analysis.one_liner: Speeds logging and fuels work on federal forests by cutting environmental review and limiting lawsuits over forest projects.
analysis.headline: The House passed the Resilient Federal Forests Act 232-188 on November 1, 2017, but the Senate Agriculture Committee never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let the Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management approve logging, salvage, and fuels-reduction projects on national forests and public lands with far less environmental study — often skipping detailed review entirely — while limiting court injunctions, cutting off attorney fees for people who sue over forest projects, and moving some disputes into arbitration. It also includes wildfire disaster declarations, tribal forest-management authority, rural school funding changes, and an exemption letting 16- and 17-year-olds work in hazardous logging jobs for a parent.
analysis.who_benefits: Timber and logging companies would get faster access to federal timber through categorical exclusions, expedited salvage sales after fires, and longer stewardship contracts. Communities near fire-prone forests would get quicker fuels reduction and reforestation. Tribes would gain new authority to manage federal forest lands within their homelands. Rural counties would gain flexibility in how they use Secure Rural Schools funds.

how_it_helps.text: Creates categorical exclusions — approval without a detailed environmental impact study — for projects up to 10,000 acres aimed at insect and disease treatment, hazardous fuel reduction, or protecting municipal water sources, and up to 30,000 acres when developed through a collaborative process [S3].

Requires salvage and reforestation plans after large catastrophic events to complete environmental assessment within 60 days, with only 30 days for public comment, and directs reforestation of at least 75 percent of burned acres within five years [S3].
Allows wildfires on federal land to be declared a major disaster, opening disaster-relief pathways for fire response [S2] [S3].
Speeds tribal requests to protect tribal forest assets, requiring an initial federal response within 120 days and completion of environmental reviews and agreements within two years [S3].

Lets rural counties use Secure Rural Schools reserve funds for firefighting, law enforcement patrols, and emergency-services training and equipment, and keeps county payments flowing as direct payments [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund wildfire disaster declarations and reforestation on public land. The public loses environmental review and legal standing: citizens challenging forest projects could not recover attorney fees, courts could not halt post-fire salvage logging, injunctions would expire after 60 days, and disputes could be forced into binding arbitration with no judicial review. Conservation groups lose their main leverage. Older teens would face newly legalized hazardous logging work.

drawbacks.text: For projects on timber-suitable lands and insect-and-disease treatment areas, the agency would study only two alternatives — do the project or do nothing — removing the range of alternatives that environmental review normally weighs [S2] [S3].

Bars courts from issuing any injunction against post-catastrophe salvage operations, caps other injunctions at 60 days, and denies attorney fees to successful challengers — mechanisms environmental groups use to enforce forest laws [S3].

Exempts forest management projects from Endangered Species Act consultation when the agency itself decides a project is not likely to harm listed species, and lets projects proceed if required consultation is not finished within 90 days [S3].
Declares forest plans exempt from the National Environmental Policy Act as 'major federal actions' and ends re-consultation when species are newly listed or new information emerges about harm [S3].
Repeals the Eastside Screens wildlife protections on national forest lands in the inland West and removes Northwest Forest Plan survey requirements in the Pacific Northwest [S3].

Amends the Fair Labor Standards Act so that 16- and 17-year-olds employed by a parent in logging or mechanized operations deemed hazardous for their age group would not be counted as engaged in oppressive child labor [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Faster fuels reduction and post-fire reforestation address a real problem: overgrown, fire-prone federal forests endanger communities and water supplies, and environmental reviews can drag out for years. But the bill gets its speed largely by removing the checks — limited alternatives, weakened endangered-species consultation, stripped injunctions, no attorney fees — that let the public catch badly designed projects, and it entrenches commercial logging as the standing answer to fire risk. The unrelated child labor provision, permitting teens in hazardous logging jobs, is a significant weakening of a worker protection bolted onto a forestry bill.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on a mostly party-line vote, but the Senate Agriculture Committee never took it up, and it expired when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Introduced by Rep. Bruce Westerman on June 20, 2017, with 18 cosponsors (16 Republicans, 2 Democrats) [S1] [S4].
The House Agriculture and Natural Resources Committees marked it up and reported it amended in October 2017, and the other two committees were discharged [S5].

On November 1, 2017, Rep. O'Halleran offered a motion to recommit — a last-chance amendment to extend Secure Rural Schools funding — which failed 189-230, with 187 of 194 Democrats supporting it and 230 of 238 Republicans opposed [S5] [S6].
Final passage passed 232-188: Republicans favored it 222-9, while Democrats opposed it 179-10 [S5] [S7].
The Senate received the bill November 2, 2017, and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry, which took no further action [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Timber companies kept the slower status quo rather than gaining expanded expedited harvesting, and conservation groups kept full access to the courts. Communities hoping for faster wildfire mitigation on federal land got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Timber firms gained nothing; conservation groups kept their lawsuits

sides.party_line_note: Passage split sharply by party: 222 of 238 Republicans voted yes and 179 of 194 Democrats voted no; even the Democratic leader's Secure Rural Schools amendment drew only two Republican votes [S6] [S7].

industries.note: The bill would give timber purchasers faster access to federal timber through categorical exclusions, expedited post-fire salvage sales, 20-year stewardship contracts, and litigation limits. Some of that harvesting doubles as fuel reduction communities want, but it also entrenches commercial logging as the standing channel for federal forest management with less public oversight.

The bill removes attorney fees for challengers, bars injunctions against post-fire salvage, caps injunctions at 60 days, and shifts disputes to binding arbitration. These groups' courtroom enforcement role, which ordinary people rely on to check federal land decisions, would be sharply narrowed.

Targeted and late-season grazing would qualify as categorical-exclusion fuel treatment, and the bill authorizes stock ponds, water catchments, and fence modifications benefiting livestock. Ranchers gain subsidized range improvements on federal land.

Title VII would let tribes treat certain federal forest lands as Indian forest land for management, require timely federal responses to tribal protection requests, and set up demonstration projects. Tribes gain direct authority over forest lands central to their homelands.

Secure Rural Schools amendments would continue direct payments, allow reserve funds for firefighting and emergency services, and shrink resource advisory committees from 15 to 9 members. Counties gain spending flexibility but lose some representation on the committees that steer the funds.
